BATCH G · BOARD 3 OF 5

Asking for help at the scale of a project

Screens 12–15. A question takes an afternoon; a collaboration takes a year. The request board, mentorship matching and events are the surfaces where a need bigger than a thread gets stated in terms someone can actually say yes to — a technique, an organism, a deadline, and what is offered in return.

WHAT A REQUEST MUST STATE
01The technique, from the controlled vocabulary
02The organism or system
03A real date, or "no fixed date" — not "urgent"
04What you offer · co-authorship, reciprocity, funding or access
05What you already have · attached, not described
FIELD 04 IS THE WHOLE DESIGN
Collaboration boards fail when they fill with people asking for unpaid work. Requiring the offer up front turns a request into a proposal, and lets the reader decide in ten seconds instead of a three-email negotiation.
EXPIRY IS AUTOMATIC
A request disappears from the board at its deadline whether or not it was matched. Nothing here rots — a board of stale asks is worse than an empty one.

13 MENTORSHIP MATCHING (C11) + OFFICE HOURS (C23) 720 × 680 · bounded commitments only
MENTORSHIP 27 mentors available · both sides opt in
WHAT YOU ARE ASKING FOR
ONE CONVERSATION · 30 min A FEW SESSIONS · 3 months ONGOING · 12 months
Every match is a bounded commitment with an end date. Nobody agrees to "mentor" an unknown person indefinitely — that is why open-ended mentorship schemes have a 70% silent-drop-off rate.

OFFICE HOURS · C23
A calendar with real slots and a stated topic scope. Lower friction than mentorship for both sides, and often all that was actually needed.
THE CONFLICT FILTER
"Nobody who could review my papers" is a first-class field. A mentee cannot speak freely to someone with power over their career, and matching them is worse than not matching at all.

ARCHIVED, NOT EPHEMERAL
The thread stays on the event page, searchable, with its artifact links live. Most conference chat is thrown away; the questions in it are often better than the talk.
ONE MODERATION RULE
Speakers can mark a message as about unpublished data, which hides it from the public archive while leaving it visible to attendees. Conferences routinely show things not yet published.

WHY POSTERS GET DOIs
A poster is often a PhD student's only citable output for two years, and it currently disappears the moment the conference ends. Minting a DOI makes it a real output: it appears on the CV export, it can be cited, and the work exists even if the paper never lands.
